html:
The Nicaraguan Literacy Campaign was a five-month drive in 1980 in which about 100,000 volunteers, most of them young students, went into the countryside to teach people to read and write.

After the revolution, around half of adults in Nicaragua could not read. The new government closed the secondary schools and sent students to live with farming families. They taught in the evenings by lantern and worked in the fields by day. Inspired by the Cuban campaign of 1961 and the ideas of the Brazilian teacher Paulo Freire, lessons were also political.

By official count the rate of illiteracy fell to about 13 percent. UNESCO gave the campaign a prize. Some volunteers were killed by Contras, and on the Caribbean coast it was later run in Miskito and English. The campaign shaped a generation of young Nicaraguans.
sum: The Nicaraguan Literacy Campaign was a five-month drive in 1980 in which about 100,000 volunteers, most of them young students, went into the countryside to teach people to read and write.
